overview.historicalContext:
Girard Desargues (1591-1661) was a French mathematician who is considered one of the founders of projective geometry. He published this theorem in 1639 in a work on conic sections. The theorem is remarkable because it is self-dual in projective geometry (the dual statement is also Desargues's theorem), it characterizes Desarguesian planes (those where the theorem holds), and it fails in some non-Desarguesian projective planes.

Desargues's theorem is fundamental to projective geometry and has applications in computer graphics, computer vision, and perspective drawing in art and architecture.
overview.problemStatement:
**Theorem (Desargues):** If two triangles ABC and A'B'C' are in **perspective from a point** (i.e., the lines AA', BB', CC' are concurrent at a point O), then they are in **perspective from a line** (i.e., the intersections P = AB ∩ A'B', Q = BC ∩ B'C', R = CA ∩ C'A' are collinear).

**Converse:** If two triangles are in perspective from a line, then they are in perspective from a point.

A projective plane where this theorem holds is called a **Desarguesian plane**.
overview.text:
This formalization proves Desargues's theorem — two triangles in perspective from a point are in perspective from a line, and conversely — using homogeneous coordinates in the projective plane. Points are represented as equivalence classes of ℝ³\{0}, lines as cross products p × q, and collinearity/concurrence reduce to determinant conditions det(p,q,r) = 0.

The proof is purely algebraic: the perspective-from-a-point condition (AA', BB', CC' concurrent) and perspective-from-a-line condition (AB∩A'B', AC∩A'C', BC∩B'C' collinear) are both expressed as determinant equations, and the implication between them follows from multilinear algebra identities. Commentary connects to the Moulton plane (a non-Desarguesian projective plane), the coordinatization theorem (Desarguesian iff coordinatizable by a division ring), and applications in computer vision. Wiedijk 100 theorem #87.
overview.proofStrategy:
Our proof uses homogeneous coordinates in the projective plane:

1. **Projective Points:** Represented as nonzero vectors in R^3, where scalar multiples represent the same point

2. **Lines:** The line through points p, q is represented by their cross product p × q

3. **Collinearity:** Three points are collinear iff the determinant of their coordinate matrix is zero

4. **Concurrence:** Three lines are concurrent iff the determinant of their coefficient matrix is zero

5. **Key Insight:** The perspective conditions translate to determinant equations that are related through the algebraic properties of cross products and determinants
keyInsights: **Projective Self-Duality:** Swapping 'point' $\leftrightarrow$ 'line' and 'concurrent' $\leftrightarrow$ 'collinear' transforms Desargues's theorem into its own converse. This duality reflects the symmetric role of points and hyperplanes in projective space.

**Algebraic Characterization:** A projective plane is Desarguesian $\iff$ it is coordinatizable by a division ring. The Moulton plane (non-Desarguesian) shows this is a non-trivial structural property, not an automatic consequence of the incidence axioms.

**Cross Product Encoding:** In $\mathbb{R}^3$ homogeneous coordinates, the line through $p, q$ is $p \times q$, and the intersection of lines $\ell, m$ is $\ell \times m$. This makes the proof purely algebraic: concurrence and collinearity reduce to determinant conditions.

**Determinant Unification:** Three points $p, q, r$ are collinear $\iff \det(p, q, r) = 0$. Three lines $\ell, m, n$ are concurrent $\iff \det(\ell, m, n) = 0$. The proof reduces both perspective conditions to related determinant equations.

**Non-Desarguesian Planes Exist:** The Moulton plane (modify the intersection rule for lines of certain slopes) satisfies all projective plane axioms but violates Desargues's theorem. This shows the theorem is independent of the basic incidence axioms — it is a genuine structural condition.
prerequisites: Linear algebra (cross products in $\mathbb{R}^3$, determinants, linear dependence)
Matrix theory ($3 \times 3$ determinants, the scalar triple product $\det(u, v, w) = u \cdot (v \times w)$)
Projective planes (incidence axioms, Desarguesian vs non-Desarguesian)

sections.title: Projective Geometry Setup
sections.summary: Definition of projective points and lines using homogeneous coordinates in R^3.
sections.mathContext: Points and lines in $\mathbb{RP}^2$ are represented as nonzero vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (up to scalar multiples). Point $p$ lies on line $\ell$ iff $p \cdot \ell = 0$ (dot product). This homogeneous coordinate model makes the point-line duality manifest.

sections.title: Fundamental Operations
sections.summary: Line through two points, intersection of two lines, and point-on-line incidence.
sections.mathContext: Line through points $p, q$: $\ell = p \times q$ (cross product). Intersection of lines $\ell, m$: $p = \ell \times m$. Point $p$ on line $\ell$: $p \cdot \ell = 0$. The cross product is the key operation: $(p \times q) \cdot p = (p \times q) \cdot q = 0$ (scalar triple product vanishes when two vectors coincide).

sections.title: Collinearity and Concurrence
sections.summary: Determinant conditions for three points being collinear or three lines being concurrent.
sections.mathContext: Three points $p, q, r$ are collinear $\iff \det(p, q, r) = 0$ (linearly dependent). Three lines $\ell, m, n$ are concurrent $\iff \det(\ell, m, n) = 0$. The algebraic symmetry between these conditions reflects the projective duality between points and lines.

sections.title: Perspective Configurations
sections.summary: Definitions of perspective from a point and perspective from a line for two triangles.

sections.title: Helper Lemmas
sections.summary: Technical lemmas about determinants, cross products, and linear dependence.

sections.title: Main Theorem
sections.summary: Desargues's theorem: point perspective implies line perspective.
sections.mathContext: Forward direction: concurrent lines $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ (i.e., $\det(A \times A', B \times B', C \times C') = 0$) implies collinear intersection points $P, Q, R$ (i.e., $\det(P, Q, R) = 0$). The key identity: $\det(P, Q, R) = \det(AA', BB', CC') \cdot K$ for an algebraic factor $K$, proved by the `ring` tactic.

sections.title: Converse Theorem
sections.summary: The converse: line perspective implies point perspective, by projective duality.

sections.title: Full Equivalence
sections.summary: The complete iff statement combining both directions.

sections.title: Special Cases
sections.summary: Example: triangles sharing a vertex are trivially in perspective from that point.

sections.title: Historical Context and Connections
sections.summary: Discussion of projective duality, non-Desarguesian planes, and applications.

conclusion.summary: This formalization establishes Desargues's Theorem using homogeneous coordinates in projective geometry. The theorem states that perspective from a point and perspective from a line are equivalent conditions for pairs of triangles. The proof uses cross products and determinants to express the geometric conditions algebraically.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: Desargues's theorem is foundational to projective geometry.

It characterizes Desarguesian planes and is closely related to the coordinatizability of projective planes by division rings. The theorem has practical applications in computer graphics (perspective projection), computer vision (3D reconstruction), and the theory of perspective in art.

crossReferences.description: Desargues's and Pascal's theorems are the two fundamental theorems of projective geometry: Desargues concerns perspective triangles, while Pascal concerns hexagons inscribed in conics — together they form the backbone of projective geometry

Both concern concurrency and collinearity in triangle configurations: Ceva's theorem characterizes cevian concurrency, while Desargues's theorem relates the perspective center (concurrency) to the perspective axis (collinearity)

The Pythagorean theorem operates in Euclidean (metric) geometry, while Desargues's theorem operates in projective geometry — the contrast illustrates how different geometric frameworks reveal different truths about figures

Both concern fundamental structural properties of geometric objects: Euler's formula constrains polyhedra topologically (V-E+F=2), while Desargues's theorem constrains triangle configurations projectively

Both are foundational results about planar geometric/combinatorial structures: the four-color theorem concerns graph coloring on the plane, while Desargues's theorem concerns projective configurations — both involve deep structural analysis

Hilbert's 4th problem asks for all metrics on a projective space where straight lines are geodesics — a question about projective geometry, the same framework in which Desargues's theorem lives. Desargues's theorem characterizes which projective planes can be coordinatized over division rings (Desarguesian planes), while Hilbert's 4th problem characterizes which metrics respect the projective line structure. Both reveal the deep interplay between algebraic structure and geometric axioms in projective spaces
